newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO differs on how many new members to invite.
newsitem.headline: NATO differs on how many new members to invite.

text.p: NATO countries differed on Thursday over how many new members from former communist Europe to invite to join the alliance when it opens its door to old foes at a special summit in Madrid next month.

During the first formal discussion of the issue at a meeting in the Portuguese town of Sintra, several states, mainly from southern Europe, expressed support for inviting as many as five new members into the West's defence group.
"Our position on this is wellknown -- we are in favour of enlarging it to five," Portuguese Foreign Minister and host of the meeting Jaime Gama told reporters.
Spain, Italy and France are also known to be in favour of a larger group which most commentators say would place Romania and Slovenia alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
But the United States, by far NATO's most important country and its paymaster, made clear it would like to keep the number down to three, arguing expansion must not weaken the alliance.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told alliance foreign ministers the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) "must continue to insist that the candidates for membership in NATO meet the highest possible standards before they are invited to join".

"The alliance should admit only those new democracies that have both cleared the highest hurdles of reform and demonstrated they can meet the full obligations of membership ... NATO enlargement is not a scholarship programme," she said.
"We want the first round of enlargement to be seen as a solid success in these terms and we want to be backed by strong parliamentary and public majorities," she said.

Five other ministers from NATO's 16 current members indicated they still had an open mind on the subject, holding out the prospect of a possible compromise on four ahead of the summit in Madrid on July 8-9.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana stressed the discussion had only just started and was confident an agreement would be found by the end of June.
"I am sure we will reach a consensus, I don't have any doubts we will reach a consensus," he told a news conference.
In an attempt to avoid creating new divisions in Europe, the alliance pledged that the door would stay open after it admitted its first new members since 1982.

"We recommend to our heads of state and government to make explicit our commitment the Alliance remains open to any other European state able and willing to fulfill the principles (of membership) and contribute to our common security," said a final communique.
The foreign ministers said the Madrid summit should "give substance to this commitment".
Apart from the five countries backed by the southern bloc, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and the former Yugoslav Repubic of Macedonia have also applied for membership.
Solana will now start work on a short list of candidates and visit their capitals to inform them of the results.

NATO has said any former communist country wishing to be considered must have established democratic control of its armed forces, set up a market economy and be attempting to make its forces compatible with those of the alliance.

But privately officials admit the decision on who to invite is essentially a political one and NATO capitals are desperate to avoid creating new tensions between those gaining admittance and those that do not.
